title: Gaussian-process-based Bayesian optimization for neurostimulation interventions in rats
author: Choinière, Guay-Hottin, et al.

steps.title: Prepare implantation and electrophysiology equipment
steps.instruction: Gather all materials required for rat implantation and EMG recording: a 32‑channel MEA and EMG wires, a surgery suite, Tucker‑Davis Technologies (BioAmp processor, EMG amplifier, stimulus isolator) with a compatible Windows computer, and a dedicated space for electrophysiologic experiments.

steps.title: Install GP‑BO library and Python environment
steps.instruction: Clone the EduOptimNeurostim repository, create a Python 3.7.4 virtual environment (via virtualenv or Anaconda), activate it, and install required packages.

substeps.instruction: Open a command prompt (GitBash on Windows).
cd to a desired folder and run: > git clone https://github.com/mbonizzato/EduOptimNeurostim.git
cd EduOptimNeurostim
Create the environment: > virtualenv --python=python3.7.4 venv
Activate it: > venv/Scripts/activate
Install dependencies: > pip install -r requirements.txt

steps.title: Create and edit config for hyperparameter calibration
steps.instruction: Copy /config/online.json to /config/config.json and edit the JSON fields to describe the data source, input space, hyperparameters to test, and optimization settings.

substeps.instruction: Set "output_path" to a folder such as "output/hyperparameter_cali_kappa".
Choose a data source:
a) Pre‑collected data – point "dataset_path" to "data/rat".
b) Semi‑synthetic data – compute the mean response for each electrode from n = 3 repetitions, add parameterised noise, and simulate n = 20 repetitions per electrode.
c) Fully synthetic data – assign plausible evoked‑response values for every electrode combination, ensuring realistic smoothness and noise levels.
Define the input space (electrode grid): "input_space": {"channel_x": [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8], "channel_y": [1,2,3,4]}.
Configure the acquisition function (UCB):
Specify optimization parameters:
"optimization": {"name": "gpbo", "max_queries": 32, "n_repetitions": 30, "n_random_steps": {"default": 1, "values": [1,2,3,4,5,7,10,15,20,25,30,32], "find_best": false}}.
If desired, add a prior:
"prior": {"path": "priors/rat_mapping_2D.mat", "scale": 0.5}.
Download the antecedent dataset (Windows requires GitBash): > bash /scripts/download_nhp_rat_dataset.sh data

steps.title: Run hyperparameter calibration (including κ search)
steps.instruction: Execute the calibration script, examine performance graphs, and select the best κ value for later online runs.

substeps.instruction: Verify the library installation works (e.g., import the package in Python).
Run the calibration command: > python main.py -c config/config.json
Wait for the job to finish (may take a while).
Open the graph in "output/hyperparameter_cali_kappa" and identify the κ value that yields the highest average performance.
Edit "config.json" to set this value as the new "default" under "kappa".

steps.title: Test hardware‑software integration with dry run
steps.instruction: Connect stimulation and recording headstages to test wires immersed in saline, run the algorithm once, and confirm a stimulation artefact appears in the recordings.

substeps.instruction: Connect the TDT stimulus isolator and EMG amplifier to test leads.
Place the leads in a saline bath.
Execute the same command used for calibration (e.g., > python main.py -c config/config.json).
Verify that a clear stimulation artefact is recorded.

steps.title: Prepare animal and connect headstages
steps.instruction: Bring the implanted rat to the electrophysiology space, ensure it is calm (sedated or habituated), and attach the stimulation and EMG headstages to the cranial connectors.

substeps.instruction: Position the animal so the hindlimb is freely suspended.
Connect the stimulation headstage to the MEA connector.
Connect the EMG wires to the selected hindlimb muscle (e.g., Tibialis Anterior).

steps.title: Execute online optimization with optimal hyperparameters
steps.instruction: Run the GP‑BO algorithm in the live animal to find the electrode that maximizes peak EMG amplitude.

substeps.instruction: Confirm "max_queries" remains set to 32 (one query per electrode).
If frequency is to be co‑optimized, extend "input_space" with "frequency": [100,200,300,400,500] and apply the modulation factors [0.52,0.94,1,1.05,1.11] to the offline data as described.
Start the online run: > python main.py -c config/config.json
During the 32 queries, keep the animal still; avoid executing queries while it moves.
Observe the evoked EMG responses after each query.

steps.title: Analyze metrics and determine optimal electrode
steps.instruction: After the online run, review the saved plots in the output folder to assess exploration vs. exploitation trends and identify the electrode (Cartesian coordinate) that yielded the maximal EMG peak.

substeps.instruction: Open the files in "output/online_rat_mapping_2D".
Record the optimal (x,y) coordinate and any additional parameter (e.g., frequency) that gave the highest response.
Return the animal to its home cage.

description: As demonstrated in the primary publication1 and elsewhere,2,3,4,5,6 Gaussian-process (GP)-based Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithms are a powerful framework to automatically optimize the efficacy of neurostimulation. It has been shown to outperform other strategies to simultaneously find the optimal values of multiple stimulation parameters (i.e., the optimal combination of parameter values) to maximize a chosen feature of the evoked response (e.g., the movement amplitude or the electromyographic [EMG] burst amplitude). The stimulation parameters can be of various nature, such as the electrode or electrical contact used to deliver the stimulation (i.e., stimulation location), the current amplitude, the pulse frequency, the pulse width or the timing of stimulation delivery during behavior. In essence, stimulation optimization consists of the identification and selection of the stimulation parameter(s) value(s) with the greatest effect (efficacy) on the chosen feature of the evoked response. As the parameters-response relationship is treated as a black box, data points from the relationship are required to realize the optimization. Consequently, the complexity of the optimization process is determined by the number of parameters simultaneously explored and the number of potential values considered for each of these parameters (i.e., combinations of parameters values). Clinically, machine learning approaches hold great promise for applications that need solving of high-dimensional optimization problems, difficult or impossible to manually solve. However, to evaluate the performance of the algorithm and demonstrate its potential in a given application, simple scenarios in which only one parameter with few possible values is optimized, are desirable. In these cases, the parameter values can be systematically explored and the ground truth of the parameters-response relationship established.
